title: Sydney Opera House
blurb: Jørn Utzon’s 1973 performing arts center on Sydney Harbour. Fourteen precast concrete shell vaults, every one a section of a single 75.2 m sphere, wear a chevron skin of more than a million Swedish tiles and rise from a pink granite podium. This detailed cutaway separates each vault into its outer surface, inner lining, tile lid bands and rib fans, and opens the podium to show the five main venues inside.

systems.name: Podium
systems.description: The monumental base, 183 m long and 120 m wide, clad in pink granite aggregate panels quarried at Tarana, holding the box office, concourses, foyers and the smaller venues.

systems.name: Concert Hall shells
systems.description: The western group of precast concrete vaults over the Concert Hall. Each vault is a section of a single 75.2 m sphere, stepping up from low entry vaults to the high stage tower.

systems.name: Opera Theatre shells
systems.description: The eastern group of vaults over the Joan Sutherland Theatre, called the Opera Theatre until 2012. Each vault is a section of a single 75.2 m sphere.

systems.name: Restaurant shells
systems.description: The smaller group of vaults on the western side of the Monumental Steps, housing the Bennelong Restaurant.

systems.name: Chevron tile lids
systems.description: Prefabricated lids bolted to the concrete ribs, carrying the 1,056,006 tiles in a chevron pattern of glossy white and matte cream.

systems.name: Glass walls
systems.description: Glass curtain walls enclosing the foyer spaces in the mouths of the vaults: 6,225 sq m of French made glass, about 2,000 panes in 700 sizes.

systems.name: Interiors
systems.description: Performance venues inside the podium and beneath the vaults, from the 2,679 seat Concert Hall with its Grand Organ to the 210 seat Utzon Room.

systems.name: Steps and terraces
systems.description: The stone paved forecourt, the Monumental Steps with individual treads, and the western broadwalk, used as an outdoor performance space.

systems.name: Structure
systems.description: The hexagonal pedestal blocks, the precast rib fans carrying the vaults, and the podium colonnades.

systems.name: Foundations
systems.description: The 588 concrete piers sunk up to 25 m below sea level, split into northern and southern fields.

explanations.concert hall auditorium volume: The Concert Hall seats 2,679 and is home to the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. It began as a multipurpose opera and concert hall, and the fitted stage machinery was later pulled out. Volume geometry is schematic.

explanations.concert hall stage deck: The stage deck of the Concert Hall with its rear wall. The major hall was originally intended as a multipurpose opera and concert hall; the stage machinery already designed and fitted was pulled out and largely thrown away. Stage geometry is schematic.
explanations.grand organ case: The case of the Sydney Opera House Grand Organ, the largest mechanical tracker action organ in the world, with over 10,000 pipes. Case geometry is schematic.
explanations.grand organ pipe facade: Schematic pipe facade of the Grand Organ. The real instrument has over 10,000 pipes and is the largest mechanical tracker action organ in the world.

explanations.joan sutherland theatre auditorium volum: The Joan Sutherland Theatre seats 1,507 and is the Sydney home of Opera Australia and The Australian Ballet. It was called the Opera Theatre until 17 October 2012. Volume geometry is schematic.
explanations.joan sutherland theatre stage deck: The stage deck of the Joan Sutherland Theatre, a proscenium theatre with 1,507 seats, the Sydney home of Opera Australia and The Australian Ballet. Stage geometry is schematic.
explanations.joan sutherland theatre pit: The orchestra pit of the Joan Sutherland Theatre. The pit is cramped and considered dangerous to musicians’ hearing. Pit geometry is schematic.
explanations.drama theatre volume: The Drama Theatre seats 544. The smaller venues sit within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.playhouse volume: The Playhouse seats 398 and sits within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.studio volume: The Studio holds up to 400 people depending on configuration and sits within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.utzon room volume: The Utzon Room seats 210. Rebuilt to Utzon’s own design and opened in 2004, it holds his tapestry Homage to Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach.
explanations.yallamundi rooms volume: The Yallamundi Rooms, a function space hosting up to 400 people, the first new venue created inside the Opera House since the Utzon Room refurbishment of 2004. Room geometry is schematic.
explanations.recording studio room: The building houses a recording studio among its other facilities; the whole building holds nearly 1,000 rooms including the five main auditoria. Layout is schematic.
explanations.the lounge venue: The Lounge is named as a venue on the official Opera House visitor map. The northern and western foyers are also used for performances on an occasional basis. Layout is schematic.

explanations.concert hall entry vault, outer surface: The low entry vault of the western group, over the Concert Hall. Each vault is a section of a single sphere 75.2 m in radius; the 14 shells of the building would combine to form a perfect sphere. Structurally they are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs, not shells in the strict sense. Vault placement and dimensions are schematic.
explanations.concert hall entry vault, inner lining: Schematic inner lining of the concert hall entry vault, shown beneath the precast shell. Interior surfaces of the real building include off-form concrete, Australian white birch plywood from Wauchope, and brush box glulam.
explanations.concert hall entry vault, tile lid, lowe: Lower band of the prefabricated tile lid over the concert hall entry vault. The vaults wear 1,056,006 tiles in two colors, glossy white and matte cream, arranged in a chevron pattern on about 4,250 prefabricated lids bolted to the ribs. The tiles were made by the Swedish company Höganäs AB; the 120 mm square Sydney Tile took three years of development, and the glossy finish lets rainwater wash the roof clean. Lid band divisions are schematic.

explanations.concert hall entry vault, pedestal block: Schematic hexagonal concrete pedestal block under the concert hall entry vault. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs; Hornibrook cast 2,400 precast ribs and 4,000 roof panels in an on site factory.
explanations.concert hall entry vault, lower rib fan: Schematic lower half of the precast concrete rib fan, running from the pedestal toward the midspan of the concert hall entry vault. Hornibrook manufactured the ribs in an on site factory, supporting them during construction with an adjustable steel-trussed erection arch developed by Hornibrook engineer Joe Bertony.
explanations.concert hall entry vault, upper rib fan: Schematic upper half of the precast concrete rib fan, running from the midspan to the apex of the concert hall entry vault. The 1961 spherical solution let arches of varying length be cast in a common mould and placed adjacent to one another to form the spherical section; the 2,194 precast sections are held together by 350 km of tensioned steel cable.

Structurally they are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs, not shells in the strict sense. Vault placement and dimensions are schematic.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, inner lining: Schematic inner lining of the opera theatre vault 3, shown beneath the precast shell. Interior surfaces of the real building include off-form concrete, Australian white birch plywood from Wauchope, and brush box glulam.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, tile lid, lower b: Lower band of the prefabricated tile lid over the opera theatre vault 3. The vaults wear 1,056,006 tiles in two colors, glossy white and matte cream, arranged in a chevron pattern on about 4,250 prefabricated lids bolted to the ribs. The tiles were made by the Swedish company Höganäs AB; the 120 mm square Sydney Tile took three years of development, and the glossy finish lets rainwater wash the roof clean. Lid band divisions are schematic.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, tile lid, upper b: Upper band of the prefabricated tile lid over the opera theatre vault 3. The vaults wear 1,056,006 tiles in two colors, glossy white and matte cream, arranged in a chevron pattern on about 4,250 prefabricated lids bolted to the ribs. The tiles were made by the Swedish company Höganäs AB; the 120 mm square Sydney Tile took three years of development, and the glossy finish lets rainwater wash the roof clean. Lid band divisions are schematic.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, pedestal block: Schematic hexagonal concrete pedestal block under the opera theatre vault 3. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs; Hornibrook cast 2,400 precast ribs and 4,000 roof panels in an on site factory.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, lower rib fan: Schematic lower half of the precast concrete rib fan, running from the pedestal toward the midspan of the opera theatre vault 3. Hornibrook manufactured the ribs in an on site factory, supporting them during construction with an adjustable steel-trussed erection arch developed by Hornibrook engineer Joe Bertony.
explanations.opera theatre vault 3, upper rib fan: Schematic upper half of the precast concrete rib fan, running from the midspan to the apex of the opera theatre vault 3. The 1961 spherical solution let arches of varying length be cast in a common mould and placed adjacent to one another to form the spherical section; the 2,194 precast sections are held together by 350 km of tensioned steel cable.
